---
title: "Departure and destination airports"
description: "How OPDI names the departure airport (adep) and the destination airport (ades) of each flight from its trajectory alone, and what adep_p, ades_p and the source columns say."
---

## In one sentence

`adep` is the airport the flight left from and `ades` the airport it flew
to, as four-letter ICAO codes, worked out from the trajectory alone, without
flight plan or schedule.

## What it needs

- The cleaned reports of the track (see
  [Cleaning of position reports](cleaning.qmd)): the first reports for the
  departure, the reports near airports below 6,000 ft for the destination.
- **Candidate airports**: the large and medium airports of OurAirports, an
  open list of the world's airports with position, elevation and whether they
  have scheduled passenger service. Small airfields and heliports are not
  candidates; records named as duplicates of another airport are left out.
- For the correction (last part below): the runway events of the track.

## How it is computed

Departures and arrivals use two methods, because the evidence differs. A
departing aircraft is usually first received on or near the runway; an
arriving aircraft is often lost by the receivers before it lands.

### Ranking candidates

1. Candidates near a report are found with a grid of H3 cells of resolution 7
   (each about 5 km²); the distance to each is then measured along the great
   circle.
2. An airport without scheduled service gets 10 NM added to its distance, so
   that a military or private field wins only when it is clearly nearest. The
   addition is not made when the aircraft is at that airport (flagged on the
   ground, or within 2 NM of it and at most 1,500 ft above it), unless an
   airport with scheduled service also lies within 2 NM.

### Departure airport: the first report

3. Take the track's first report and the nearest candidate (ranked as above).
4. Name it when the report is at most **30 NM** from it and the aircraft is on
   the ground or at most **15,000 ft** above the airport's elevation.
5. A first report in the air (more than 1,000 ft above the airport and not
   flagged on the ground) names no airport when the track descends in its
   first 180 s (the altitude changes by less than −200 ft): it is an arrival
   first received on its descent.
6. `adep_p` lists the other candidates within 30 NM of the first report, in
   the order of the ranking.

### Destination airport: the altitude trend

7. Take every report within **30 NM** of a candidate and at most
   **6,000 ft** above its elevation.
8. Smooth the barometric altitude over 5 consecutive reports (about 25 s).
9. Each report votes: climbing if the smoothed altitude went up since the
   previous report, descending if it went down. When descending votes
   outnumber climbing ones, the flight landed at that airport.
10. Of the airports it landed at, only those whose last nearby report is
    within 600 s of the latest landing compete (a stop earlier in the track
    does not). Among them the nearest wins, ranked as above; when two are less
    than 2 NM apart, the one the aircraft's course points at wins.
11. `ades_p` lists other candidate airports near the end of the track,
    nearest first.

### Correction from the runway events

12. After the events are computed, a runway event can replace an airport.
    The airport of a departure runway event (`ATOT`, `line-up` or
    `take-off-roll`) replaces `adep` only if it is the first departure event of
    the track and lies within 30 NM of the track's first report with a
    position. The airport of an arrival runway event (`ALDT` or
    `runway-vacated`) replaces `ades` only if it is the last arrival event,
    comes after every departure event, and lies within 30 NM of the last
    report with a position. A runway-window time (`info.method` = `legacy`)
    never replaces an airport.
13. The source columns say how each airport was decided: `aerodrome` (from the
    trajectory), `runway_event` (from step 12), `out_of_area` or
    `undetermined` (no airport, as for an overflight).

`OOA` (out of area) is written only in data built for the European area: it
means the track began (or ended) within 30 NM of the edge of that area, so
the flight came from (or went to) outside it. With the default worldwide
coverage the area has no edge, and such a flight has no airport.

## Based on

- Developed for OPDI.
- Airports come from [OurAirports](../resources.qmd#ref-ourairports) and the search grid is
  [H3](../resources.qmd#ref-h3).

## What is published

Flight list columns `adep`, `ades`, `adep_p`, `ades_p`, `adep_source` and
`ades_source` (see the [Data dictionary](../data/dictionary.qmd#flight-list)).
The same columns are repeated on every row of the flight events file.

## Use cases

- **Traffic between airport pairs**: count flights per `adep` and `ades`,
  using the movement columns to avoid counting pieces twice.
- **Choose by confidence**: `adep_source` = `runway_event` means the aircraft
  was seen on a runway of that airport, the most reliable case.
- **Check alternatives**: near airports close together (a city with several
  airports), `adep_p` and `ades_p` show the other candidates.

## Limitations

Small airfields and heliports are never named; an arrival lost far from its
destination gets no `ades`; a track holding several flights names only its
first and last airports. See
[Limitations: airports](../limitations.qmd#lim-airports).

## Availability and accuracy

Availability is the share of flights with an airport; accuracy is the share
of the flights the Network Manager records whose OPDI airport equals the
recorded one.
